title: Chandipura Virus Death Toll Rises to 22 Children in Gujarat as Monsoon Outbreak Intensifies
excerpt: Gujarat has reported 63 suspected cases and 12 confirmed infections this monsoon season, with health officials ordering emergency vector control across affected districts.
body:
• The death toll from the Chandipura virus outbreak in Gujarat has risen to 22 children this monsoon season, according to state health officials and multiple Indian news reports.
  • Gujarat has reported 63 suspected cases with 12 confirmed positive for the virus; seven children remain under treatment.
  • The state has intensified vector control, trained nearly 2,000 pediatricians, and deployed medical teams for door-to-door screening in affected districts.
  • Chandipura is a rare but highly lethal vector-borne virus transmitted by sandflies, primarily affecting children under 15.

A Worsening Outbreak

The Chandipura virus has killed 22 children in Gujarat this monsoon season, with the death toll more than doubling over the past three weeks as the outbreak spread across multiple districts, according to reports from The Hindu and The Indian Express citing state health officials.

Gujarat Health Minister Praful Pansheriya confirmed that the state has recorded 63 suspected cases so far this year. Of those, 12 have tested positive for the virus, and eight deaths have been officially attributed to confirmed infections. The remaining fatalities are suspected to be linked to the virus, with laboratory results pending for several samples.

Cases have been reported from Gandhinagar, Sabarkantha, Kheda, Aravalli, Panchmahal, and Banaskantha districts. The most recent fatality involved a two-year-old girl from Rajasthan who died on July 19 while receiving treatment at Banas Medical College in Gujarat's Banaskantha district.

What Is the Chandipura Virus?

Chandipura vesiculovirus (CHPV) is a rare rhabdovirus first identified in Maharashtra's Chandipura village in 1965. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected sandflies — small insects that breed in cracks, animal shelters, and organic debris during the monsoon. The virus can also spread through ticks and mosquitoes.

The infection predominantly affects children under 15 and can progress rapidly from fever and body aches to acute encephalitis — inflammation of the brain — within hours. The case fatality rate in past outbreaks has ranged from 55% to 75%, making it one of the deadliest vector-borne infections in India.

"Laboratory testing for the accurate diagnosis of the Chandipura virus is progressing rapidly. Of the 27 suspected cases initially, results for 19 have been received."

— Praful Pansheriya, Gujarat Health Minister

State Response

Gujarat has launched an emergency response that includes door-to-door screening in affected villages, insecticide spraying and dusting in areas where sandflies have been detected, and the deployment of medical teams to district and civil hospitals.

The state has trained 1,993 pediatricians on Chandipura virus detection and treatment protocols. Health officials have directed private clinics and smaller health centers to provide immediate primary care and refer suspected cases without delay to hospitals equipped with oxygen and ventilator facilities.

Authorities have also completed preventive measures at all 61 locations where Chandipura virus cases were reported in Gujarat during the 2024 monsoon season, which saw a smaller outbreak.

Advice for NRI Families

Diaspora families planning monsoon-season visits to Gujarat — particularly to rural areas in the affected districts — should take precautions to minimize sandfly exposure. These include using insect repellent, sleeping under bed nets, and keeping children away from animal shelters and areas with organic debris where sandflies breed.

Parents should seek immediate medical attention if children develop sudden high fever, seizures, or altered consciousness during or after a visit to affected areas. Early intervention is critical, as the virus can progress to encephalitis within hours.
